plot_extraction.response_text:
At a winter ball, cultured novelist Aston Tyrrell and young artist Topsy Garrick retreat to a tropical conservatory. Each is accompanied by personified aspects of the self: Aston’s crude lust, Cain, and cynical intelligence, Sir Jasper; Topsy’s sensuality, Belle, and frightened innocence, Henrika. They initially converse through dummies representing their conventional social masks, but soon abandon them and discover a shared interest in literature. Aston offers to critique Topsy’s poetry, while their hidden impulses comment on and manipulate the flirtation.

As they explore the conservatory’s grotesque, animate flowers, intoxicating music, heat, perfume, and a chloroform-producing plant weaken Topsy’s resistance. Aston supports and tenderly kisses her, but Cain then embodies the predatory desire behind his cultivated behavior by forcing a kiss on her. Topsy’s innocent aspect recoils in terror, and Aston, suddenly ashamed, drives Cain away and begs forgiveness. Topsy coldly ends the incident and insists it be forgotten.

Unable to confront what has happened, Aston and Topsy recover their dummies and resume empty small talk as they return to the ballroom. Their inner companions follow, while the sinister flowers mockingly chuckle after them.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story is written as a one-act theatrical farce rather than as conventional prose fiction. It opens with an elaborate scenic description, proceeds through stage directions and character-labelled dialogue, and ends with the formal descent of the curtain. The implied narrator functions partly as dramatist and partly as sardonic master of ceremonies, occasionally intruding with arch comments such as “I regret to say.” This creates a deliberately artificial, self-aware atmosphere in which the characters appear less like psychologically rounded individuals than personified fragments of desire, inhibition, vanity, and social convention.

The tone combines sophisticated satire, erotic grotesquerie, decadent fantasy, and broad comedy. Polite upper-class courtship is treated as a brittle performance concealing appetite, calculation, embarrassment, and fear. The humour often depends on the collision between refined language and bodily impulse: literary conversation and “purely æsthetic” admiration coexist with lust, sweat, perfume, faintness, teeth, blood, and predatory flowers. The text maintains an amused, cynical distance from its characters, allowing moments of apparent tenderness or remorse while undermining them through heckling alter egos, mechanical dummies, or bathos. Its comedy can become deliberately cruel, and its representation of Cain relies on racist caricature, plantation dialect, and dehumanising imagery characteristic of offensive period stereotypes.

The diction is highly stylised and wide-ranging. Scenic passages employ lush, sensuous, almost fin-de-siècle vocabulary—“palpitating,” “serpentine,” “suppurating,” “languorous,” “chryselephantine”—while the spoken exchanges mimic fashionable social chatter, cultivated literary discourse, childish exclamations, and pseudo-scientific exposition. Learned references to Freud, Mendel, Darwin, Henry James, Humboldt, Aristophanes, and botanical taxonomy lend the comedy an intellectual veneer. These references are rarely neutral: they parody cultivated self-consciousness and the tendency to disguise instinct in the language of art, science, and moral responsibility. Invented botanical names such as the “twangum tree,” “kadapoo tree,” and “Alocusia Cantatrix” mix plausible nomenclature with nonsense, strengthening the mock-scholarly tone.

The imagery is dense, visual, tactile, olfactory, and frequently anatomical. The conservatory is imagined as a feverish erotic ecosystem filled with flowers that possess eyes, tongues, breasts, teeth, skins, tentacles, and throats. Similes turn vegetation into wounds, spiders, traps, predatory animals, and machines. Scents, heat, music, colour, and bodily movement work together to produce an atmosphere of intoxication. The central visual contrast is between the frozen black-and-white landscape outside and the humid, coloured interior: frost and death oppose tropical fertility, yet the apparent vitality within is also threatening, diseased, and carnivorous. This makes the setting both literal stage scenery and an externalisation of repressed sexual life.

Sentence style varies according to function. The opening description uses long, cumulative sentences packed with semicolons, appositions, catalogues, and escalating detail. Stage directions are often similarly expansive, choreographing facial expressions, gestures, dances, lighting effects, and shifts in bodily control with novelistic precision. Dialogue is generally short and rhythmically repetitive, especially when reproducing strained small talk: “a very good band,” “a perfect floor,” and “at the Necropole” recur as empty social formulas. Ellipses, pauses, exclamations, parenthetical instructions, and repeated phrases convey hesitation, trance, excitement, or embarrassment. Cain’s “nyum nyum,” Jasper’s mocking commentary, Belle’s eager prompting, and Henrika’s fearful protests operate as recurring verbal motifs.

Characterisation is allegorical and divided. Aston and Topsy each carry a dummy representing their socially acceptable public persona, while the surrounding “family” members embody impulses and internal voices. Cain represents crude appetite, Jasper detached intelligence and self-mockery, Belle sensual curiosity and manipulation, and Henrika innocence, fear, and vulnerability. The device literalises psychological conflict: decorous conversation is conducted through puppets while desire and commentary hover visibly around the speakers. The characters repeatedly speak across or over one another, producing a layered theatrical effect in which outward behaviour, inward motive, and critical interpretation are all presented at once.

The dialogue is structured around irony. Aston’s elevated compliments, professional generosity, and concern for “the cause of Art” are exposed by Jasper as rehearsed seduction tactics. Topsy’s apparent independence and intellectual seriousness coexist with susceptibility to flattery, while Belle actively stages her sister’s attractiveness. Euphemism and aesthetic language continually conceal sexual motives, only for the alter-ego figures to state or enact those motives openly. After the crisis, the principals return to their dummies and resume banal ballroom conversation, suggesting that social etiquette does not resolve experience but mechanically covers it over.

The plot develops through controlled escalation. It begins with awkward small talk, moves into intellectual flirtation, then into increasingly sensual music, perfume, touch, dizziness, and physical intimacy. The tour of fantastic flowers supplies a sequence of comic set pieces while also functioning as seduction: each botanical curiosity intensifies the atmosphere and narrows the distance between Aston and Topsy. The chloroform plant makes the metaphor of intoxicated desire literal. The kiss brings the suppressed conflict into open violence and terror, after which remorse, denial, and etiquette restore the social surface. The circular ending repeats the opening conversation almost verbatim, reinforcing the sense that the characters are trapped in ritualised behaviour.

The dominant techniques are grotesque personification, parody, repetition, bathos, symbolic doubling, mock-scientific invention, and metatheatricality. The flowers react like an audience, screaming when exposed to frost and chuckling after the humans leave; the final hiccough reduces the evening’s cultivated erotic drama to a gross bodily joke. The story’s overall style is therefore extravagant, theatrical, intellectually playful, and satirically merciless. Beneath its fantasy lies a sustained critique of cultivated manners as puppetry: civilisation supplies elegant phrases and graceful poses, but appetite, vanity, predation, shame, and fear remain visibly active behind them.

## THE ORCHID AND THE ALIBI  
### A Farce in One Act

**PERSONS**

**ASTON TYRRELL**, a novelist of cultivated reputation.  
**SIR JASPER**, his intelligence, polished by use and blunted by amusement.  
**CAIN**, his appetite, without education but not without eloquence.  
**ASTON’S DUMMY**, dressed faultlessly and capable of six opinions.

**TOPSY GARRICK**, a young painter who also writes verses.  
**BELLE**, her sensual curiosity, adventurous and smiling.  
**HENRIKA**, her innocence, perpetually expecting thunder.  
**TOPSY’S DUMMY**, charming, correct, and almost entirely hollow.

**THE FLOWERS**, who have never read Freud, but understand him.

---

### THE CONSERVATORY AT LADY MUMBLEDOWN’S WINTER BALL

Beyond the glass, December lies embalmed in moonlight. The park is a black-and-white engraving: iron trees scratch a pewter sky; snow upholsters the statues; a fountain, arrested in mid-compliment, holds out crystal fingers from which nothing falls. Here and there a carriage lamp creeps along the drive like a yellow beetle condemned to punctuality.

Within the conservatory, however, Nature has been allowed champagne.

The atmosphere is green, gold, crimson, humid, palpitating, and faintly indecent. Great leaves overlap like the ears of prehistoric elephants. Orchids hang from branches in postures which would be prohibited in sculpture. A serpentine creeper, purple as a bishop’s private intention, coils round a marble Diana and inserts a tendril beneath her lifted arm. The ponds are lacquered black; lilies float upon them with the complacency of ladies who know that their shoulders are admirable. From the ballroom comes the muffled convulsion of a waltz—violins sighing, cornets protesting, drums enforcing morality.

Among the vegetation are several botanical celebrities. There is the **Alocusia Cantatrix**, whose scarlet throat sings when stroked; the **Twangum Tree**, covered with little bladder-like fruits which explode at compliments; the **Kadapoo**, a pale, pendulous plant reputed to exhale chloroform when emotionally disturbed; and the **Mendelia Duplex**, whose blossoms reproduce, with scientific accuracy, the worst characteristics of both parent plants.

At the back, two doors lead to the ballroom. Beside each stands a gilt chair.

Enter **ASTON**, carrying his **DUMMY** under one arm. The Dummy resembles him as a successful portrait resembles its purchaser: the brow is nobler, the waist smaller, the expression better connected.

Behind Aston come **SIR JASPER** and **CAIN**.

Sir Jasper is thin, silver-haired, elegant, and appears to have been born leaning against a mantelpiece. Cain is broad, red-handed, impatient, and dressed in a dinner coat that seems continually on the point of splitting from honest disagreement with civilisation.

ASTON places his Dummy upright.

**ASTON’S DUMMY.** What a very good band.

**ASTON.** Not yet.

**DUMMY.** I beg your pardon.

**SIR JASPER.** It has been saying that all evening. At dinner it praised the soup during the fish.

**CAIN.** Why bring it?

**ASTON.** Because society is alarmed by sincerity.

**CAIN.** Leave society. Find a woman.

**SIR JASPER.** He has found several. It is keeping them which has proved literary.

**ASTON.** I came here for air.

**SIR JASPER.** You came because Miss Garrick came.

**CAIN.** Same thing.

**ASTON.** Miss Garrick interests me professionally.

**SIR JASPER.** Naturally. She is twenty-two.

**CAIN.** Yellow hair.

**ASTON.** Her work—

**CAIN.** Yellow hair.

**ASTON.** —shows a certain freshness.

**SIR JASPER.** Yellow hair.

**ASTON.** You are both intolerable.

**SIR JASPER.** We are both you.

The right-hand door opens. Enter **TOPSY**, carrying her **DUMMY** by the waist. Belle and Henrika follow. Topsy wears a white gown with silver embroidery. Belle wears the same gown as it imagines itself at midnight. Henrika wears it as it was described to Topsy’s aunt.

Topsy sets her Dummy upon the second chair.

**TOPSY’S DUMMY.** What a very good band.

**ASTON’S DUMMY.** And a perfect floor.

**TOPSY’S DUMMY.** Are you going to the Necropole on Thursday?

**ASTON’S DUMMY.** I believe so.

The Dummies smile. Their smiles remain after the occasion has passed.

**TOPSY.** Oh! Mr Tyrrell.

**ASTON.** Miss Garrick.

**BELLE.** He followed us.

**HENRIKA.** Let us go back.

**TOPSY.** I did not know you had left the ballroom.

**ASTON.** I did not know it myself until the air improved.

**SIR JASPER.** Opening number seven: atmospheric coincidence.

**CAIN.** Stand nearer.

Aston moves half a pace nearer.

**HENRIKA.** He moved!

**BELLE.** So did she.

Topsy has also moved, though in the opposite direction; owing to the geometry of flirtation, this brings them closer.

**ASTON.** It is intolerably crowded.

**TOPSY.** Lady Mumbledown says she invited only intimate enemies.

**ASTON.** There must be eight hundred.

**TOPSY.** She is very affectionate.

They laugh.

The **Twangum Tree** inflates three blue fruits and pops them softly.

**TOPSY.** What was that?

**ASTON.** Approval.

**SIR JASPER.** Do not be modest. It may have been indigestion.

**TOPSY.** Your latest novel has made everyone terribly unhappy.

**ASTON.** Then it has fulfilled its social purpose.

**TOPSY.** I cried over the duchess.

**SIR JASPER.** He did not.

**ASTON.** I am touched.

**CAIN.** Touch her.

**ASTON.** The duchess was intended less as a woman than as a symbol of—

**SIR JASPER.** A woman who did not answer his letters.

**TOPSY.** I thought she was Desire pursued by Responsibility.

**ASTON.** Exactly.

**SIR JASPER.** Aston was Responsibility. Desire escaped at Boulogne.

**BELLE.** Ask him about the poems.

**HENRIKA.** Don’t! They are in the blue notebook.

**BELLE.** Which she brought.

**HENRIKA.** By accident.

**BELLE.** In her glove.

Topsy thrusts her left glove behind her.

**ASTON.** You write yourself, I believe?

**TOPSY.** Paint.

**BELLE.** And write.

**TOPSY.** Only paint.

**HENRIKA.** Tell the truth.

**TOPSY.** Sometimes I write things which are not exactly writing.

**ASTON.** That is how most books begin.

**TOPSY.** Little verses.

**ASTON.** Ah.

His “Ah” is deep, encouraging, experienced, and has been used upon manuscripts, soufflés, and moral difficulties.

**SIR JASPER.** Opening number twelve: the great man stoops to the budding talent.

**ASTON.** May I see them?

**TOPSY.** Certainly not.

**BELLE.** Yes.

**HENRIKA.** No!

**TOPSY.** They are absurd.

**ASTON.** Absurdity is merely truth in its evening clothes.

**SIR JASPER.** That sentence was rejected from his last novel for excessive meaning.

**TOPSY.** They are very modern.

**ASTON.** Then they need not scan.

**TOPSY.** They do not.

**ASTON.** Or rhyme.

**TOPSY.** They cannot.

**ASTON.** Or communicate.

**TOPSY.** They refuse.

**ASTON.** My dear Miss Garrick, you are already celebrated.

Topsy laughs. Belle slips the blue notebook from the glove and places it in Aston’s hand.

**TOPSY.** Belle!

**ASTON.** Thank you.

**TOPSY.** I did not give it to you.

**ASTON.** Then I am doubly grateful.

**HENRIKA.** Take it back.

**BELLE.** Let him keep it overnight.

**HENRIKA.** Why overnight?

**SIR JASPER.** Because morning has such excellent legal advisers.

Aston opens the book.

**TOPSY.** Not here!

He shuts it.

**ASTON.** I shall read it reverently.

**CAIN.** In bed.

**ASTON.** With professional care.

**SIR JASPER.** In bed.

**ASTON.** And send you a frank opinion.

**SIR JASPER.** He will say: “There is something here.” There is always something there. Generally a meeting.

**TOPSY.** I do want honesty.

**ASTON.** Honesty is the one luxury an established artist can afford.

**SIR JASPER.** Since he no longer practises it.

The ballroom music grows louder, then dissolves into a languorous measure. The conservatory lights turn amber. Several flowers unclose moistly.

**BELLE.** How warm it is.

**HENRIKA.** Too warm.

**CAIN.** Good.

**TOPSY.** What extraordinary plants.

**ASTON.** Lady Mumbledown’s late husband collected them.

**SIR JASPER.** He died of botany in Sumatra.

**ASTON.** This, for example, is the Alocusia Cantatrix.

He indicates a fleshy flower, vermilion at the lip and gold within. Its stamens tremble like the eyelashes of a contralto awaiting applause.

**TOPSY.** Does it really sing?

**ASTON.** If sympathetically approached.

**TOPSY.** How does one approach a flower sympathetically?

**CAIN.** Show her.

**ASTON.** One touches the lower petal.

He strokes it with one finger. The flower emits a low, voluptuous note: “O-o-oh.”

Topsy starts. Belle claps. Henrika covers her ears.

**TOPSY.** How dreadful!

**BELLE.** Again.

**ASTON.** Humboldt considered its song a form of self-defence.

**SIR JASPER.** Humboldt was frequently abroad.

Topsy extends her hand, hesitates, and touches the petal. The flower ascends an octave and sings a phrase of the waltz.

**TOPSY.** It knows the tune!

**ASTON.** Plants have no taste, but excellent memories.

Nearby, a spotted blossom opens an eye.

**TOPSY.** That one is looking at us.

**ASTON.** The Oculata Moralis. It watches everything and understands nothing. Botanists believe it related to the chaperon.

The blossom blinks severely.

**HENRIKA.** I dislike it.

**BELLE.** It dislikes us. That is much more stimulating.

They proceed down a path between enormous leaves. The companions follow: Belle beside Topsy, Cain beside Aston, Henrika and Sir Jasper bringing up the rear like Conscience and the Review Press.

**TOPSY.** Did you always mean to write novels?

**ASTON.** No. At twenty I intended to reform humanity.

**TOPSY.** What happened?

**ASTON.** I met it.

**SIR JASPER.** At twenty-five he intended to understand women.

**ASTON.** Jasper—

**SIR JASPER.** At thirty he reduced his ambitions and described them.

**TOPSY.** It must be wonderful to understand people.

**ASTON.** One need only notice what they conceal.

**TOPSY.** And what do I conceal?

**HENRIKA.** Nothing.

**BELLE.** Everything.

**CAIN.** Ask closer.

Aston looks at Topsy. She meets his gaze, then looks toward the frozen garden.

**ASTON.** A good deal of courage.

**TOPSY.** Conceal courage?

**ASTON.** The world forgives a pretty woman almost anything except fearlessness. So she learns to blush while she conquers it.

Belle smiles triumphantly. Henrika blushes for Topsy.

**SIR JASPER.** Very neat. He once used it on a suffragist in a gondola.

**TOPSY.** You say such finished things.

**ASTON.** They are unfinished until believed.

**TOPSY.** I am not sure I believe them.

**ASTON.** Then I shall have to improve them.

The **Twangum Tree** bursts six fruits in a row: pop, pop, pop, pop, pop, pop.

**SIR JASPER.** The house applauds.

**TOPSY.** And what do you conceal?

**ASTON.** My age.

**TOPSY.** Besides that.

**ASTON.** My opinions.

**TOPSY.** Besides those.

**CAIN.** Me.

Aston glances toward Cain.

**ASTON.** An hereditary barbarian.

**TOPSY.** How interesting.

**SIR JASPER.** She thinks he means an ancestor.

**CAIN.** Tell her I am alive.

**ASTON.** We all possess a certain primitive remnant. Darwin gives him a tail; Freud gives him a sofa; society gives him opera gloves and hopes for the best.

**TOPSY.** And does the best happen?

**ASTON.** Almost never. That is why there are novels.

They reach the **Mendelia Duplex**. Its paired blossoms are grotesquely dissimilar: one white, smooth, and virginal; the other striped, hairy, and equipped with minute teeth. As they watch, the white blossom bites the striped one.

**TOPSY.** Oh!

**ASTON.** Mendel would have been delighted.

**SIR JASPER.** Mendel was a monk.

**BELLE.** The white one did it.

**HENRIKA.** Perhaps it was frightened.

**CAIN.** Teeth are teeth.

A gust of cold air enters through an imperfect pane. A row of orchids shrieks in tiny soprano voices and folds itself up. Aston removes his coat and places it over Topsy’s shoulders.

**TOPSY.** I am not cold.

**ASTON.** The orchids are.

**TOPSY.** Then give it to them.

**ASTON.** They have compromised themselves already.

She keeps the coat.

**BELLE.** It smells of him.

**HENRIKA.** It smells of tobacco.

**BELLE.** Precisely.

The music becomes softer. The leaves move though there is no wind. A moon-coloured flower droops above Topsy and releases a thread of perfume.

**TOPSY.** What is that scent?

**ASTON.** The Kadapoo.

**SIR JASPER.** Stand back.

**ASTON.** A harmless narcotic.

**SIR JASPER.** So is flattery, in professional hands.

**TOPSY.** Narcotic?

**ASTON.** Only when the plant is emotionally disturbed.

**TOPSY.** How does one disturb a plant emotionally?

At once Cain pinches one of its stems. The Kadapoo quivers. A pearl of clear liquid swells at its throat and bursts into vapour.

**CAIN.** Like that.

**ASTON.** Cain!

**TOPSY.** What did you say?

**ASTON.** “Careful.”

**TOPSY.** I feel rather—

She sways.

Henrika screams. Belle catches Topsy’s train but not Topsy. Aston supports her at the waist.

**ASTON.** You are faint.

**TOPSY.** No. Only the room has become unreliable.

**SIR JASPER.** It has taken lessons from the company.

**HENRIKA.** Take her back!

**BELLE.** Not yet.

**ASTON.** Breathe slowly.

**TOPSY.** I am breathing slowly.

**CAIN.** Slower.

**ASTON.** Look at me.

She does. The waltz enters through the glass in broken pulses. The Alocusia hums accompaniment. A great crimson blossom expands behind them like an anatomical diagram of a heart.

**TOPSY.** Your face is moving.

**ASTON.** I regret to say it has done so for years.

**TOPSY.** You have kind eyes.

Sir Jasper looks appalled.

**SIR JASPER.** Intoxication is no excuse for inaccuracy.

**ASTON.** Sit here.

He guides her to a marble bench. Belle arranges the coat round her shoulders and draws one shining lock of hair forward. Henrika attempts to push it back. The lock travels between them like a disputed frontier.

**TOPSY.** I must look idiotic.

**ASTON.** You look—

**SIR JASPER.** Take care.

**CAIN.** Say beautiful.

**ASTON.** —very young.

**TOPSY.** That is worse.

**ASTON.** Very beautiful.

**SIR JASPER.** There. The familiar catastrophe.

**TOPSY.** That is better.

She closes her eyes.

**HENRIKA.** Topsy, open them.

**BELLE.** Keep them closed.

**TOPSY.** I can hear everybody thinking.

**ASTON.** What do they say?

**TOPSY.** The flowers say we are absurd.

A circle of orchids inclines toward them.

**ASTON.** Flowers are notorious realists.

**TOPSY.** Belle says—

She stops.

**ASTON.** Who is Belle?

**TOPSY.** Nobody.

Belle kisses Topsy’s ear.

**TOPSY.** She says you will kiss me.

A pause. Even the ballroom band appears to lean upon the dominant seventh and listen.

**HENRIKA.** No!

**CAIN.** Yes.

**SIR JASPER.** We have now reached the portion omitted from the memoirs.

**ASTON.** And what do you say?

**TOPSY.** I say Belle is vulgar.

**BELLE.** Coward.

**ASTON.** Then Belle is mistaken.

He bends and kisses Topsy’s forehead with grave tenderness. It is a beautiful action, admirably lit, and would have satisfied any audience not paying attention.

Topsy opens her eyes.

**TOPSY.** Oh.

**BELLE.** That was not what I meant.

**CAIN.** Nor me.

**ASTON.** Forgive me.

**TOPSY.** For that?

**ASTON.** For everything it may have meant.

**SIR JASPER.** An ingenious insurance policy.

Topsy rises, still unsteady.

**TOPSY.** You make even apologies sound like prefaces.

**ASTON.** It is a professional disease.

**TOPSY.** And is tenderness another?

**ASTON.** No.

For one instant Aston is quiet, unguarded, and almost a human being. Sir Jasper turns away with distaste. Henrika watches hopefully. Belle becomes still.

Cain does not.

He steps behind Aston, thrusting close as a shadow at sunset. His hands close over Aston’s arms; his face appears beside Aston’s face, coarser, hungrier, stripped of syntax.

**CAIN.** Enough words.

**ASTON.** Go away.

**CAIN.** She stayed.

**ASTON.** She is faint.

**CAIN.** She spoke of kissing.

**ASTON.** She trusted me.

**CAIN.** Same door. Different label.

**SIR JASPER.** Aston, this scene is deteriorating.

**CAIN.** Nyum, nyum. Perfume. Hair. Mouth.

He drives Aston forward.

Aston catches Topsy by the shoulders and kisses her mouth violently.

For a second Belle flares scarlet with startled triumph—then recoils. Henrika gives a thin, tearing cry. Topsy struggles. The Oculata Moralis opens all its eyes. The toothed Mendelia snaps. The Alocusia emits a hideous high note. Outside, the black trees remain perfectly decorous.

Topsy tears herself free. A bright line of blood marks her lower lip.

Silence.

Cain licks his own lip and laughs.

**CAIN.** There.

Aston stares at Topsy, then at his hands, as if both have been translated into a language he has always pretended not to know.

**HENRIKA.** Don’t touch us! Don’t touch us!

She clings to Topsy. Belle stands behind them, pale and sickened.

**TOPSY.** You hurt me.

**ASTON.** I—

**CAIN.** We.

**ASTON.** No.

He turns on Cain.

**ASTON.** Get out.

**CAIN.** You called.

**ASTON.** Get out!

**CAIN.** You fed me compliments, perfume, dark paths, fainting. Now the plate comes, you blame the knife.

Aston strikes him. Cain staggers into the Twangum Tree. Its fruits explode like pistol shots. Cain laughs once more, but less confidently.

**ASTON.** Out!

Cain retreats among the leaves. As he goes, the plants bend toward him, recognising a relative. At last he disappears behind the Kadapoo, though his breathing remains audible.

Sir Jasper examines his fingernails.

**SIR JASPER.** Violence against one’s instincts is generally postponed until after their success.

**ASTON.** Be silent.

**SIR JASPER.** Certainly. Intelligence is always dismissed when testimony becomes inconvenient.

He withdraws a few paces.

Aston approaches Topsy, but Henrika thrusts out both arms.

**HENRIKA.** No nearer.

Aston stops.

**ASTON.** Miss Garrick—

**TOPSY.** Do not.

She wipes the blood from her lip with Aston’s white handkerchief. The small stain spreads into a rose, vulgar and undeniable.

**ASTON.** There is no excuse.

**TOPSY.** No.

**ASTON.** I thought—

**SIR JASPER.** You did not.

**ASTON.** I allowed—

**TOPSY.** Do not make grammar of it.

He bows his head.

**ASTON.** Forgive me.

**TOPSY.** You said that before.

**ASTON.** Before, it was vanity. Now—

**TOPSY.** Now it is discomfort.

**ASTON.** Shame.

**TOPSY.** That is discomfort with a mirror.

Belle looks at Topsy with admiration. Henrika continues trembling.

**ASTON.** I would give anything—

**TOPSY.** You have given me a criticism already.

She holds out her hand.

**TOPSY.** My notebook.

Aston produces it. For a moment he clutches it, not from desire to keep the poems but from the human tendency to retain some object when one has forfeited the person. Then he returns it.

**ASTON.** I shall never forgive myself.

**TOPSY.** That sounds exhausting. You will manage by breakfast.

**ASTON.** You are cruel.

**TOPSY.** I am being concise.

The ballroom strikes up a polka of invincible stupidity. Through the doors comes laughter, bright and mechanical.

**TOPSY.** This did not happen.

**ASTON.** But—

**TOPSY.** It did not happen. You followed me here. We discussed flowers. I felt faint. You fetched me water.

**ASTON.** I did not.

**TOPSY.** Then you may begin by fetching it now.

Aston pours water from a silver jug beside the pond. His hand shakes. He offers the glass without approaching. Belle takes it and gives it to Topsy.

**TOPSY.** Thank you.

**ASTON.** Must it be forgotten?

**TOPSY.** It will not be forgotten. It will be denied. That is entirely different.

**SIR JASPER.** Admirable. She has learnt society in one lesson.

**HENRIKA.** I want to go home.

**BELLE.** We must go back first.

**HENRIKA.** Back there?

**BELLE.** Especially there.

Topsy removes Aston’s coat and lays it on the bench. Belle repairs her hair. Henrika wipes her lip. The stain remains faintly visible.

**TOPSY.** Is it noticeable?

**BELLE.** Only if anyone looks.

**SIR JASPER.** Nobody at a ball looks. They merely observe.

Topsy crosses to her Dummy. Aston crosses to his. They stand behind the puppets and insert their hands beneath the satin backs. The Dummies wake at once, smiling with the horrible freshness of things without memory.

Cain crawls from behind the Kadapoo and takes his place at Aston’s shoulder. A red fruit is stuck in his hair. Aston does not look at him.

Sir Jasper resumes his place. Belle stands behind Topsy, suddenly older. Henrika follows with both hands over her heart.

**TOPSY’S DUMMY.** What a very good band.

**ASTON’S DUMMY.** And a perfect floor.

**TOPSY’S DUMMY.** Are you going to the Necropole on Thursday?

**ASTON’S DUMMY.** I believe so.

**TOPSY’S DUMMY.** Lady Mumbledown’s conservatory is quite delightful.

**ASTON’S DUMMY.** Quite.

**TOPSY’S DUMMY.** Such curious flowers.

**ASTON’S DUMMY.** Purely æsthetic.

**SIR JASPER.** Naturally.

**CAIN.** Nyum.

Aston jerks his Dummy’s head toward Cain.

**ASTON’S DUMMY.** I beg your pardon?

**TOPSY’S DUMMY.** I said it is very warm.

**ASTON’S DUMMY.** Oppressively.
